title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Laboratory Interpretation—Reference Ranges, Trends & Critical Results
html:
Laboratory results are clinical cues, not stand-alone diagnoses. Safe interpretation connects the correct client and specimen with the reported value, unit, local reference interval, previous results, symptoms, medications, treatments, and timing. The RN recognizes urgent patterns, assesses the client, addresses immediate risk within scope, communicates clearly, and evaluates the response.

Learning goals

  • Verify client, specimen, timing, units, reference interval, and result reliability before interpreting a value.
  • Distinguish reference intervals, abnormal results, and organization-defined critical results.
  • Interpret common CBC, chemistry, kidney, glucose, and coagulation findings as patterns and trends.
  • Recognize collection and handling problems that can distort results.
  • Prioritize the client’s condition over an isolated number while responding promptly to time-sensitive findings.
  • Document notification, read-back, interventions, and reassessment.

Start with the client, then validate the result

When a concerning result appears, rapidly assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, vital signs, symptoms, and relevant safety risks. A symptomatic client may need immediate intervention before a repeat specimen is collected. Conversely, an unexpected value that conflicts with the client’s condition may reflect a collection, labeling, timing, or processing problem—but it must never be dismissed without assessment and follow-up.

Use the report in front of you
Reference intervals and units vary by laboratory, method, population, age, pregnancy status, and clinical context. Compare the result with the interval and unit printed on that report, then integrate the client’s baseline, trend, symptoms, orders, and treatment goals.

Reference interval is not the same as safe or expected

A reference interval describes values found in a defined comparison population. A result outside it is not automatically a diagnosis, and a value within it does not rule out illness. Therapeutic targets may differ from general reference intervals. A critical value is an organization-defined result associated with potential immediate danger and a required communication pathway; it is not simply any value marked high or low.

Before acting, verify the client identifiers, test name, specimen source, collection time, result time, unit, reference interval, fasting or medication timing when relevant, and whether the result is preliminary, corrected, or final. Compare with previous values and ask what changed: the client, the treatment, the specimen, or the measurement.

Check whether the specimen can answer the question

Preanalytic problems occur before testing and can create misleading results. Examples include wrong-client or incomplete labeling, collection from an infusing line, contamination, hemolysis, clotting in an anticoagulated tube, insufficient volume, wrong container, prolonged tourniquet use, delayed transport, incorrect temperature, and failure to follow fasting or timed-test instructions.

Hemolysis can falsely alter several analytes, including potassium, depending on the method and degree. A potassium result flagged as hemolyzed must be interpreted with the client’s condition, electrocardiographic findings when indicated, kidney function, medications, and local recollection policy. Never assume every high potassium is false, and never treat a questionable isolated result without considering immediate clinical risk.

Point-of-care testing also requires correct technique, quality control, meter identification, usable test strips, and awareness that poor peripheral perfusion can make capillary results unreliable. When a bedside result does not fit the client’s condition, assess the client and obtain confirmatory testing according to policy without delaying treatment of an emergency.

Read a complete blood count as connected cell lines

Hemoglobin and hematocrit contribute to assessment of oxygen-carrying capacity and red-cell concentration. A falling trend with bleeding symptoms, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnea, chest discomfort, pallor, or altered mental status is more urgent than a stable chronic value without symptoms. Hemoconcentration and hemodilution can change measured concentration without an equivalent change in total red-cell mass.

White blood cell count and differential support assessment of infection, inflammation, marrow function, medication effects, and immune status. A total count alone does not prove or exclude infection. Absolute neutrophil count may better describe bacterial infection risk in neutropenia; fever in a severely neutropenic client requires prompt protocol-based evaluation.

Platelet count supports primary clot formation. Interpret the number with active bleeding, petechiae, invasive procedures, medications, and trend. A sudden platelet fall can matter even before the value reaches a general critical threshold. Platelet clumping or a clotted specimen can produce an inaccurate result and may require recollection.

Interpret electrolytes through their clinical effects

Sodium reflects water balance relative to body sodium and strongly affects neurologic function. Rapid or severe change may cause headache, confusion, seizures, or reduced consciousness. Prioritize neurologic assessment, fluid history, intake and output, glucose, medications, and the rate of change. Correction must follow a prescribed plan because overly rapid correction can cause neurologic injury.

Potassium affects cardiac and neuromuscular function. Both high and low values can cause weakness and dangerous dysrhythmias. Review the ECG or cardiac rhythm when indicated, kidney function, urine output, acid-base status, gastrointestinal losses, medications, replacement therapy, and specimen hemolysis. Escalate a critical or symptomatic result promptly and do not independently improvise replacement or lowering therapy.

Calcium and magnesium influence neuromuscular and cardiac function. Albumin can affect total calcium interpretation; ionized calcium more directly reflects the physiologically active fraction. Abnormal magnesium can coexist with potassium or calcium abnormalities and make correction more difficult. Assess for weakness, cramps, paresthesias, reflex changes, seizures, and rhythm disturbance according to the cue cluster.

Connect kidney markers with perfusion and output

Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine help assess kidney function but are affected by more than one process. Creatinine trend and estimated glomerular filtration rate support interpretation of filtration, while BUN can also change with hydration, protein breakdown, gastrointestinal bleeding, and other factors. A rising creatinine with falling urine output, hypotension, edema, or nephrotoxic exposure needs prompt evaluation.

Never declare kidney function normal from one value alone. Review baseline, age and muscle mass context, intake and output, daily weight, hemodynamics, urinalysis, medications, contrast exposure, and dose-adjustment needs. Report significant trends and protect the client from further harm through the prescribed care pathway.

Interpret glucose with symptoms and treatment timing

Connect serum or capillary glucose with meals, enteral feeding, insulin or other medications, activity, illness, and symptoms. Sweating, tremor, hunger, headache, irritability, confusion, seizure, or decreased consciousness can accompany hypoglycemia. Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, blurred vision, or altered breathing and mental status can accompany severe hyperglycemia.

For a low bedside glucose, assess the client and follow the hypoglycemia protocol immediately; do not wait for symptoms to worsen. Choose oral or non-oral treatment according to consciousness and swallowing safety, then repeat glucose at the protocol-defined time and determine why the event occurred. A completed intervention without reassessment leaves the safety loop open.

Understand coagulation tests in context

Prothrombin time and INR primarily assess the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways and are commonly used to monitor warfarin therapy. Activated partial thromboplastin time assesses the intrinsic and common pathways and may be used for unfractionated heparin monitoring, although some settings use anti-Xa assays. Therapeutic goals are client- and indication-specific.

Interpret coagulation results with the medication, last dose or infusion rate, target ordered, bleeding or thrombosis signs, liver function, platelet count, procedures, and specimen quality. Blood drawn from a heparinized line can be contaminated and falsely prolong a result. Active bleeding with hemodynamic instability takes priority over waiting for a repeat test.

Use clusters, trends, and time

A single abnormal result asks, “Is this real, relevant, and urgent?” A trend asks, “Which direction and how fast?” A cluster asks, “Which physiologic process could connect these cues?” For example, vomiting plus falling potassium, rising bicarbonate, weakness, and ectopy suggests a clinically meaningful pattern; an isolated value cannot provide the same picture.

Compare values collected under similar conditions when possible, but do not delay urgent action to create a perfect comparison. Review interventions between results—fluids, diuretics, transfusion, electrolyte replacement, insulin, dialysis, bleeding, surgery, or specimen timing—because a trend without its treatment context can be misleading.

Respond to critical and unexpected results

  1. Recognize: Review the result, flag, unit, specimen information, and trend.
  2. Assess: Evaluate the client and the physiologic risk related to the result.
  3. Protect: Initiate immediate protocol or ordered safety measures within scope.
  4. Communicate: Use the required critical-result pathway and a concise SBAR; state symptoms, trends, treatments, and relevant data.
  5. Verify: Read back critical information and clarify new orders. Recollect only when indicated without postponing urgent care.
  6. Evaluate: Reassess symptoms, monitoring, and repeat results at the expected time.

If a provider does not respond and the client remains at risk, follow the chain of command. Document the result, client assessment, time and recipient of notification, read-back, orders, interventions, and response. Recording “provider aware” without this information is incomplete.

Delegation and accountability

Trained assistive personnel may collect selected specimens or perform point-of-care testing under policy and report results. The RN verifies unexpected findings, assesses the client, interprets trends, determines urgency, initiates nursing actions, communicates critical information, and evaluates outcomes. The RN cannot delegate clinical interpretation or follow-up accountability.

Clinical example

A client receiving a potassium-wasting diuretic reports weakness and palpitations. The potassium result is below the laboratory’s critical threshold. The RN assesses vital signs and rhythm, stops unsafe activity, confirms the result and specimen details, reviews urine output and medications, activates the critical-result pathway, implements prescribed monitoring and replacement, and reassesses rhythm, symptoms, and the repeat result. The RN does not treat the number in isolation or leave the response undocumented.

Use the current laboratory report, client-specific orders, organizational policy, and qualified clinical supervision. This lesson is not clinical decision support.
